source.title: CTRL: Clustering Training Losses for Label Error Detection

record.tranche_reason: The study records per-sample losses during training on corrupted labels and reports clean/noisy loss trajectories, testing the early-learning pattern conceptually. It does not run the original fully random-label experiment.
record.gate_note: The authors state that deep networks can fit random labels in the introduction, but that is background, not a result of this study. The study's own loss-trajectory result on CIFAR-100 bears on V6. Its noisy-label test-accuracy tables bear partly on V4, but do not report training error for those runs. Results from other cited work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study directly measures clean versus noisy training-loss trajectories, testing V6 despite its main purpose being label-error detection. Baseline test accuracies also bear on V4's test-degradation component, but cannot establish perfect training fit.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the loss-trajectory observation, but omits the paper's main conclusion: CTRL detects label errors effectively on image and tabular datasets, and removing detected erroneous samples generally improves retrained test accuracy. Eventual learning from every sample is stated for the Figure 2 discussion, not demonstrated numerically across all experiments.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains networks on datasets with simulated or real-world label errors and tracks loss trajectories for label-error detection; it does not use fully random labels as in the original experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Loss trajectories vary by dataset and class; the authors report that training hyperparameters and model capacity affect the loss gap and overfitting.
record.problems: For the claim-relevant evidence, the loss-trajectory example is described for one CIFAR-100 condition and plotted without numeric curve values. The noisy-label tables report test accuracy but not training error, and do not test fully random labels.
record.rows_left_out: Selected only baseline test-accuracy entries for CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 at the stated conditions. Other dataset, noise-rate, sparsity, and method rows in Tables II–VI and VIII–X are omitted because of the 60-row limit and because they do not add a direct test of the fully random-label claim.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, zero or near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Training-time overhead for fitting random versus true labels and convergence speed across corruption fractions. Reported runtime comparisons concern detection methods.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit across noise levels and degradation through fully random labeling to chance. The baseline tables cover only limited corruption ranges.
Whether explicit regularization prevents random-label fitting and whether removing it harms true-label generalization.
A separate comparison of true-label training with completely random-label training; quantitative memorization timing across models.

missing.what: The study's own theoretical loss-gap result: under balanced binary Gaussian-mixture data, independent label flips below 50%, zero initialization, and bounded log loss, Equation (3) bounds the early-learning noisy-minus-clean loss gap. This supports the early separation component of V6, without proving eventual memorization.

The authors report finding similar clean/noisy loss gaps in every dataset they experimented with. Record this as a qualitative cross-dataset observation, without inferring numeric trajectories or eventual memorization for each dataset.
missing.locator: Section III-A, immediately after the discussion of Figure 2

record.verdict_notes: No V4 verdict is assigned: the selected baseline results show test-accuracy degradation over limited noise ranges, but leave the defining perfect-training-fit component unresolved. This missing measurement is not evidence against V4. The study is not an original source for any claim version.

versions.untested_parts: No experiment trains on a completely random labeling or reports its training error and test error.
No comparison of training time or convergence speed across true and randomly labeled data or increasing corruption fractions.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
No reported training error showing perfect fit at each noise rate; noise is not swept from none to all. Test-accuracy results are represented by selected rows.
The study uses weight decay for image models but does not test whether regularization prevents fitting random labels or whether removing it harms true-label generalization.
The reported result concerns clean versus noisy labels under simulated label noise, not completely random labels; no separate experiment compares learning of real and random labels.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Recorded per-sample training losses each epoch and compared average loss trajectories for clean and noisy labels.
rows.measure: Average training-loss trajectories over training; clean-label loss decreases while noisy-label loss stays roughly constant initially, then the model learns from every sample.
rows.value: The average loss gap is evident during most of training; the authors state that the model eventually learns from every sample.
rows.note: The text describes the figure and its result; the exact plotted values are not reported.
rows.check: The qualitative trajectory description is supported by Section III-A. Eventual learning from every sample is the authors' interpretation; no numeric zero-training-error result is supplied.
